list.listitem: Approximately 3% of patients with hypertension have a secondary cause. B

Suspect secondary hypertension in patients with early onset (<30 years of age), with sudden worsening of control, or with refractory response to therapy, and also in patients with abnormal screening tests on initial presentation (K+, Ca++, creatinine, or urinalysis). C

Initial diagnostic tests include MR angiogram, CT angiogram, or Doppler ultrasound for renal artery stenosis, dexamethasone suppression test for Cushing's, 24-hour urine aldosterone for hyperaldosteronism, and polysomnography for sleep apnea syndrome. C
For treatment recommendations, see chapters on individual conditions causing secondary hypertension (renal artery stenosis, Cushing's disease, aldosteronism, and sleep apnea).B

background.definition: Secondary hypertension refers to patients with an identifiable cause of hypertension. All other patients are said to have essential hypertension.

list.listitem: In a random sample of 7455 Swedish men between the ages of 47 and 54 years, 1159 were hypertensive. Of those men, a systematic evaluation found that 40 (3.4%) had secondary hypertension: 25 with renal parenchymal hypertension, 4 with renovascular hypertension, and 11 with other types of secondary hypertension. More recently, obstructive sleep apnea has been recognized as one of the most common causes of secondary hypertension.
The prevalence of secondary hypertension is more common in patients with resistant hypertension than in the overall hypertensive population.
In children with hypertension, secondary hypertension was present in 9% in primary care settings and 44% in referral settings.
More common Sleep apnea Renal parenchymal disease Renovascular hypertension (renal artery stenosis) Primary aldosteronism and other mineralocorticoid states Drug-induced or drug-related (see )

Less common Certain foods and supplements (see ) Thyroid or parathyroid disease Cushing's syndrome and other glucocorticoid excess states Obstructive uropathy Coarctation of the aorta Pheochromocytoma

Hyperaldosteronism: In Primary aldosteronism, hypertension is mediated by increased aldosterone, leading to increased retention of sodium and water and decreased renin and urinary excretion of potassium; in secondary hyperaldosteronism, hypertension is due to elevated renin.

Renal artery stenosis: Hypertension presents typically after age 50 in patients with risk factors for atherogenesis; 65% of hypertension is due to atherogenesis of renal arteries and the remainder due to fibromuscular dysplasia, which typically present younger (age 25-50 years).
Renal parenchymal disease: Hypertension results from glomerular damage, which leads to a low-renin state; eventually elevated parathyroid hormone and erythropoietin worsen the hypertension.
Cushing's syndrome: Hypertension is due to mineralocorticoid effects of glucocorticoids.
Pheochromocytoma and drug-induced: Hypertension is due to catecholamine or sympathomimetic effects.

Thyroid disease: Hypothyroidism induces decreased cardiac output, with resulting increased vascular tone and increased diastolic blood pressure; hyperthyroidism increases cardiac output and then decreases vascular tone, leading to increased systolic blood pressure.
Obstrucive sleep apnea: Hypertension results from hypoxia-induced sympathetic activation and catecholamine release.
United States Preventive Services Task Force recommends that clinicians screen adults 18 years and older for high blood pressure. A

There are currently mixed recommendations for screening for high blood pressure in children. The American Academy of Pediatric recommends routine screening for children 3 years and older, while the Academy of Family Physicians found insufficient evidence for or against routine screening in children. A

To screen for secondary hypertension, order serum potassium, serum calcium, serum creatinine, and urinalysis in patients with newly diagnosed hypertension or sudden change in hypertension control or severity. Also explore symptoms that might suggest undiagnosed or undertreated obstructive sleep apnea. C

A systematic review supports family history of secondary hypertension, prematurity, age 6 years or younger, low body weight (<10%) microalbuminuria, and serum uric acid concentration of 5.5 mg/mL or less as the most useful findings for an increased likelihood of secondary hypertension in adolescents and children.A
Suspect secondary hypertension when basic initial workup for essential hypertension (potassium, calcium, urinalysis, creatinine) are abnormal. C

Suspect secondary hypertension when patients have sudden or severe onset hypertension, have poor response to appropriate treatment, or their previously well-controlled hypertension becomes difficult to control. C
If renal artery stenosis is suspected, order duplex ultrasound, CTA (if normal renal function), or MRA. C
Review medications, foods, and supplements as possible causes of hypertension and for interference with antihypertensive therapy. C

Consider secondary hypertension generally in patients with onset before age 30 without family history; resistant hypertension; severe hypertension or hypertensive urgency; target organ damage; or a sudden increase in blood pressure when previously stable.

Consider primary aldosteronism PA in patients with any of the following: BP higher than 140/90 despite 3 antihypertensives, or BP lower than 140/90 while taking 4 antihypertensives; hypertension plus hypokalemia; hypertension and adrenal incidentaloma; hypertension and sleep apnea; hypertension and a family history of early-onset hypertension; and any first-degree relatives with confirmed PA who are also hypertensive.

A systematic review of 23 studies found that family history of secondary HTN (LR+ 4.6), weight <= 10th percentile for age and sex (LR+ 4.5) and age at diagnosis <= 5 years (LR+ 2.6) were the best predictors of secondary hypertension in children.

Consider specific causes of secondary hypertension when patients report headache, palpitations, pallor, and perspiration (pheochromocytoma); snoring or daytime somnolence (sleep apnea); heat or cold intolerance (thyroid disease); or repeated episodes of flash pulmonary edema (renal artery stenosis).

Physical examination findings that suggest secondary causes of hypertension include abdominal bruit (50% of patients with renal artery stenosis); decreased lower extremity blood pressures (aortic coarctation); and truncal obesity, purple striae, or goiter (Cushing's syndrome).

Consider secondary hypertension in patients with hypokalemia (primary aldosteronism); hypercalcemia (hyperparathyroidism); or abnormal urinalysis, serum creatinine, or anemia (renal parenchymal disease).
Guidelines from ACC/AHA (2025) now recommend evaluation for primary aldosteronism in all patients with resistant hypertension.
A 20% or more increase in creatinine during the first 2 weeks of ACE-I or ARB therapy is 100% sensitive and 70% specific for bilateral renal artery stenosis (LR+ 3.3, 0.014).

If primary aldosteronism is suspected, the initial test is a plasma aldosterone-renin ratio, obtained at least 2 hours after awakening, and after the patient has been seated comfortably for approximately 10 minutes. Withdraw any agents that markedly affect the plasma aldosterone-renin ratio (spironolactone, eplerenone, amiloride, and triamterene, potassium-wasting diuretics, and licorice) for at least 4 weeks. There is no need for confirmatory testing in patients with hypokalemia, an undetectable plasma renin level, and a plasma aldosterone concentration greater than 20 ng/dL (550 pmol/L). For other patients consider a confirmatory test (oral sodium loading test, a captopril challenge test, or a saline infusion test). If diagnosed with PA an adrenal CT should be performed.

See for suggested evaluation of causes of secondary hypertension based on clinical suspicion or abnormal screening laboratory tests. Duplex ultrasound, CT angiogram (if normal renal function), or MR angiogram is recommended for evaluation of possible renal artery stenosis.
Plasma and urine fractionated metanephrines are recommended if pheochromocytoma is suspected, followed by localization with CT or MRI if there is biochemical evidence of tumor.
In children with hypertension, a systematic review found that the presence of microalbuminuria is strongly predictive of a secondary cause.

A clinical rule has been developed to predict the likelihood of renal artery stenosis. Key predictors include smoking, recent onset hypertension, hyperlipidemia, bruit, comorbid cardiovascular disease, and male gender.
Patients with newly diagnosed hypertension should have serum potassium, serum creatinine, serum calcium, and urinalysis to screen for secondary causes.
Suspect secondary hypertension in patients with sudden worsening or poor control despite adequate therapy, and age of onset under 30.
See for differential diagnosis, typical presentation, and suggested confirmatory testing.

Aggressive treatment of hypertension and diabetes is critical to preserve function in renovascular disease. A
RCTs to date have not established the superiority of balloon angioplasty compared to medical therapy for renal artery stenosis.B
For treatment recommendations, see chapters on individual conditions causing secondary hypertension (renal artery stenosis, Cushing's disease, aldosteronism, and sleep apnea).B
Modest salt reduction for 4 or more weeks is associated with improvements in systolic blood pressure.B
The prognosis for secondary hypertension is dependent on the underlying condition. C
Patients with kidney disease should have their blood pressure lowered to less than 130/80 to 140/90, with the exact threshold varying based on guidelines and comorbidities. A

feature.caption: Differential Diagnosis of Secondary Hypertension and Suggested Confirmatory Testing.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnosis Key Distinguishing Features Confirmatory Testing
Chronic kidney disease Comorbid diabetes, increased prevalence in black race, long standing hypertension that worsens, abnormal urinalysis or serum creatinine, decreased glomerular filtration rate 24-hour urine for creatinine and protein; ultrasound of kidneys
Coarctation of aorta Decreased pressure in lower compared with upper extremities, diminished or delayed femoral pulses Transthoracic Echocardiogram, CT angiography
Cushing's syndrome Central obesity, moon facies, striae, weproximal muscle akness, thecchymoses, in skin, fatigue, acne, menstrual irregularities A 24-hour urinary-free cortisol value 4x greater than upper limit of normal or overnight low dose dexamethasone suppression test
Drug induced See for medications that can elevate blood pressure Trial off medication if possible
Hyperparathyroidism Unexplained hypercalcemia Simultaneous serum parathyroid hormone and serum calcium levels
Hyperthyroidism Tachycardia, palpitations, weight loss, heat intolerance TSH
Hypothyroidism Cold intolerance, constipation, lethargy, hair loss or coarseness TSH
Pheochromocytoma Labile or paroxysmal hypertension; episodic symptoms (headaches, pallor, palpitations, panic attacks, tachycardia, diaphoresis); a family history of MEN-II, Von Hippel Lindau, or von Recklinghausen's; or incidental suprarenal mass Plasma and urine fractionated metanephrines; localization with CT or MRI
Primary hyperaldosteronism Unexplained hypokalemia or adrenal tumor ("incidentaloma") Ratio of plasma aldosterone concentration to plasma renin activity >20, followed by confirmatory testing (eg, captopril or fludrocortisone suppression test or 24-h urinary aldosterone level)
Renal artery stenosis Onset of hypertension under 30 years, bruit, smoking, elevated serum creatinine, comorbid cardiovascular disease, flash pulmonary edema, renal failure induced by ACEI or ARB, renal failure of uncertain cause accompanied by no proteinuria and normal urinary sediment Duplex ultrasound, CT angiogram (if normal renal function), or MR angiogram
Sleep apnea Loud snoring, obesity, thick neck, daytime sleepiness Polysomnogram
